module.title: Unit 12: Playing by the Rules: Reported Speech & Sport Rules
module.objective: Mampu membicarakan izin dan aturan, memberikan instruksi sederhana, serta menggunakan struktur 'be allowed to/let' dan third conditional untuk menjelaskan situasi hipotesis di masa lalu

subModules.title: Reading Mission: Playing by the Rules and Sports
subModules.grammarFocus: Be allowed to, let, and Third Conditional

content.summary: Welcome to Unit 12. In this reading mission, you will explore texts about sports rules, school discipline, and how societies enforce rules. You will practice reading strategies such as scanning for key details and understanding permissions and past hypothetical results.

linguisticTarget.grammar: Using 'be allowed to', 'let', and the Third Conditional for past hypothetical results.
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Key terms related to discipline, punishment, breaking rules, and sports regulations.
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Scanning texts for specific rule conditions and skimming paragraphs for general themes.

learningObjectives: Understand the main idea of short B1 texts about sports and social rules.
Locate specific details such as permissions and consequences of breaking rules.
Recognize and practice grammar patterns involving modal permissions and the third conditional.

contextWarmup.prompt: What do you usually have to do when you join a new sports team?
options: Follow the team rules and respect the coach
Ignore all instructions and play alone
Change the rules whenever you feel like it
contextWarmup.explanation: Joining any team requires following established rules and respecting the coach to maintain fair play.

rules: Use 'be allowed to' + base verb to talk about permissions. Example: I'm not allowed to stay out late.
Use 'let' + object + base verb to express permission granted by someone. Example: My parents let me go to parties.
Use the Third Conditional ('If + past perfect, would have + past participle') to talk about past hypothetical situations.

commonTrap.explanation: Learners often mix up 'allow' and 'let' structures by forgetting the infinitive 'to' with 'allowed' or adding 'to' after 'let'.
commonTrap.wrong: They allowed me go. / They let me to go.
commonTrap.correct: They allowed me to go. / They let me go.

grammarFormulas.title: Sentence Patterns with Third Conditional
grammarFormulas.description: Assemble sentence blocks to practice past hypothetical outcomes:

items.exampleSentence: I'm not allowed to stay out late.
At the sports academy, discipline is extremely important.
The referee gave a severe punishment for the bad foul.
You must face the consequences if you break the rules.
Players who break the rules will receive a yellow card.
If I hadn't listened to my coach, I would have got into trouble.
My little brother is always getting told off for arriving late.
Driving without a seatbelt is against the law.

paragraphs: Every sport has its own unique set of regulations. In football, players are not allowed to touch the ball with their hands unless they are the goalkeeper inside the penalty area. If a player breaks the rules, the referee stops the match and awards a free kick or a penalty. Discipline is vital for every team member.

In the past, school sports and historical games had even stricter regulations. If students had ignored the academy discipline, they would have faced severe punishments. Today, coaches let players express their skills, but respecting the referee remains essential to avoid getting into trouble.

keyPhrases.note: Used to describe having permission to do something.
Followed directly by the bare infinitive without to.

subModules.title: Writing Mission: Rules and Past Hypotheses

content.summary: Practical guide on writing sentences about permission, rules, and past hypothetical situations using be allowed to, let, and the third conditional.

blueprintItems.title: Step 1: Expressing Permission and Rules
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + be (not) allowed to + base verb + complement
blueprintItems.example: Players are not allowed to touch the ball with their hands.

blueprintItems.title: Step 2: Using 'Let' for Permission
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + let(s) + object pronoun + base verb
blueprintItems.example: The referee lets the players drink water during the break.

blueprintItems.title: Step 3: Writing Third Conditional Sentences
blueprintItems.formula: If + past perfect, would have + past participle
blueprintItems.example: If our team had practiced harder, we would have won the match.

mechanicsRules.rule: Always place a comma after the 'if' clause when it comes at the beginning of a conditional sentence.
mechanicsRules.badExample: If we had followed the rules we would have won.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: If we had followed the rules, we would have won.
mechanicsRules.why: A comma separates the dependent condition clause from the main result clause.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use the correct auxiliary verb form for 'be allowed to' according to the subject.
mechanicsRules.badExample: He are not allowed to play in the tournament.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: He is not allowed to play in the tournament.
mechanicsRules.why: The verb 'be' must agree with the singular third-person subject 'He'.

mechanicsRules.rule: Capitalize the first letter of every new sentence and proper sports nouns.
mechanicsRules.badExample: we play football according to fifa rules.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: We play football according to FIFA rules.
mechanicsRules.why: Sentences begin with capital letters, and acronyms or proper organizations like FIFA are capitalized.

sampleSentences.en: Are we allowed to wear trainers inside the gymnasium?
sampleSentences.id: Apakah kami diizinkan memakai sepatu training di dalam gimnasium?
sampleSentences.focus: Interrogative form of be allowed to

sampleSentences.en: My coach does not let us skip the warm-up session.
sampleSentences.id: Pelatih saya tidak mengizinkan kami melewatkan sesi pemanasan.

sampleSentences.en: If the referee had seen the foul, he would have blown his whistle.
sampleSentences.id: Jika wasit melihat pelanggaran itu, dia akan meniup peluitnya.

sampleSentences.en: She wouldn't have broken her arm if she had worn protective gear.
sampleSentences.id: Dia tidak akan mematahkan lengannya jika dia mengenakan perlengkapan pelindung.
sampleSentences.focus: Result clause first in third conditional

mechanicsChallenges.keyRule: Use 'are' with plural subjects like 'Students' and capitalize the first letter.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Change the affirmative sentence into a sentence using 'be allowed to':
practicumQuestions.promptText: You can park your car in this zone.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'are allowed to' with the base verb.
targetAnswers: You are allowed to park your car in this zone.
You're allowed to park your car in this zone.
practicumQuestions.explanation: To express permission equivalent to 'can', use the subject pronoun followed by 'are allowed to' and the base verb.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using 'let' instead of 'allowed to':
practicumQuestions.promptText: The teacher is not allowed to use her phone in class.
targetAnswers: The school rules don't let the teacher use her phone in class.
Her boss doesn't let her use her phone in class.
practicumQuestions.explanation: When rewriting with 'let', the authority figure becomes the subject, followed by 'let' or 'lets' and the object pronoun.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Complete the third conditional sentence with the correct form of the verbs in brackets:
practicumQuestions.promptText: If we (train) harder, we would have won the match.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use the past perfect tense for the 'if' clause.
targetAnswers: If we had trained harder, we would have won the match.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The third conditional requires 'had' plus the past participle ('had trained') in the if-clause.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Correct the capitalization and punctuation errors in the sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: if tom had listened to the coach he would scored a goal
practicumQuestions.hint: Capitalize the name and add a comma after the condition clause.
targetAnswers: If Tom had listened to the coach, he would have scored a goal.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Proper nouns ('Tom') must be capitalized, a comma is required after the 'if' clause, and the result clause needs 'would have' plus past participle.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Change the following sentence into the negative form using 'be allowed to':
practicumQuestions.promptText: Children are allowed to swim in the deep end of the pool.
targetAnswers: Children are not allowed to swim in the deep end of the pool.
Children aren't allowed to swim in the deep end of the pool.
practicumQuestions.explanation: To make 'be allowed to' negative, simply add 'not' after the auxiliary verb 'am/is/are/was/were'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Answer the question using a full sentence with 'be allowed to':
practicumQuestions.promptText: Are guests allowed to bring pets into the restaurant?
targetAnswers: No, guests are not allowed to bring pets into the restaurant.
No, guests aren't allowed to bring pets into the restaurant.
practicumQuestions.explanation: A complete negative answer uses 'No, [subject] are not allowed to' followed by the rest of the action.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Complete the third conditional sentence in reverse order:
practicumQuestions.promptText: We would have missed the start of the movie if we (not take) a taxi.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use the negative past perfect form: had not / hadn't taken.
targetAnswers: We would have missed the start of the movie if we hadn't taken a taxi.
We would have missed the start of the movie if we had not taken a taxi.
practicumQuestions.explanation: In the negative past perfect for third conditionals, use 'had not' or 'hadn't' plus the past participle ('taken').

practicumQuestions.instruction: Transform this rule into a sentence using 'let':
practicumQuestions.promptText: My parents permit me to go out on Saturday nights.
targetAnswers: My parents let me go out on Saturday nights.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The verb 'let' is followed directly by the object pronoun ('me') and the bare infinitive ('go') without 'to'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Fix the grammatical errors in this sentence about rules:
practicumQuestions.promptText: players is not allowed touch the ball with their hands in football.
practicumQuestions.hint: Check subject-verb agreement and the preposition needed before the verb 'touch'.
targetAnswers: Players are not allowed to touch the ball with their hands in football.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Plural subject 'Players' requires 'are', and 'allowed' must be followed by the infinitive marker 'to' before the verb 'touch'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Write a third conditional sentence explaining what would have happened if you had overslept this morning:
practicumQuestions.promptText: If I had overslept this morning...
practicumQuestions.hint: Complete with a result clause starting with 'I would have...'
targetAnswers: If I had overslept this morning, I would have missed my bus.
If I had overslept this morning, I would have been late for school.
If I had overslept this morning, I would have missed the meeting.
practicumQuestions.explanation: A complete third conditional sentence combines 'If + past perfect' with 'would have + past participle' in the main clause.

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: Playing by the Rules & Reporting Speech

content.summary: Master the articulation of modal verbs, reporting verbs, and sentence stress when discussing sports rules, permissions, and past consequences in B1 spoken English.
content.audioGuidance: Pay close attention to sentence stress on key vocabulary items such as allowed, punishment, and consequences. Keep unstressed grammar words like to, be, and have weak and short.

pillars.name: Modal Reduction
pillars.explanation: Auxiliary and modal verbs such as 'can', 'must', and 'have to' are often pronounced with weak vowel sounds in natural connected speech.

pillars.name: Reporting Verb Intonation
pillars.target: Clear pitch change on reporting clauses
pillars.explanation: When reporting what someone said, raise your voice slightly on the reporting verb to signal the transition to indirect speech.

pillars.name: Consonant Linking
pillars.explanation: Link the final consonant of a reporting verb to the vowel sound of the next word, for example saying 'told_us' as one fluid unit.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: Notice how the stress shifts between the second syllable in allowed and the first syllable in discipline.
Both nouns place primary stress on the first syllable with secondary stress on the final part.
Content words like rules and trouble carry the main sentence stress while prepositions and articles remain weak.
In phrasal verbs and prepositional phrases, stress falls heavily on the lexical verb and the final noun.

drills.targetText: We are not allowed to break the rules during the match.
drills.phonetic: /wiː ɑː nɒt əˈlaʊd tuː breɪk ðə ruːlz ˈdjʊərɪŋ ðə mætʃ/
drills.focus: Clear articulation of modal permission and linking
drills.hint: Pronounce 'not allowed' clearly without dropping the final d sound.

drills.targetText: The referee told the players that they had broken the rules.
drills.phonetic: /ðə ˈrefəri təʊld ðə ˈpleɪəz ðæt ðeɪ hæd ˈbrəʊkən ðə ruːlz/
drills.focus: Reported speech intonation and past perfect verbs
drills.hint: Pause slightly after the reporting verb 'told' for natural pacing.

drills.targetText: If the team had played better, they would not have lost.
drills.phonetic: /ɪf ðə tiːm hæd pleɪd ˈbetə, ðeɪ wʊd nɒt hæv lɒst/
drills.focus: Third conditional stress and auxiliary reduction
drills.hint: Reduce 'would have' to 'would've' in spoken conversation.

drills.targetText: Breaking school discipline can lead to serious consequences.
drills.phonetic: /ˈbreɪkɪŋ skuːl ˈdɪsəplɪn kæn liːd tuː ˈsɪəriəs ˈkɒnsɪkwənsɪz/
drills.hint: Maintain equal pacing across discipline and consequences.

practicumQuestions.phonetic: /juː ɑː nɒt əˈlaʊd tuː juːz ðəʊz məˈʃiːnz ənˈles ə kəʊtʃ ɪz ˈpreznt/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use 'be allowed to' correctly to explain permissions and prohibitions.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Pronounce a sentence focusing on vocabulary related to rules and consequences.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Say this sentence clearly: Breaking sports rules often leads to severe punishment and negative consequences.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Breaking sports rules often leads to severe punishment and negative consequences.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ˈbreɪkɪŋ spɔːts ruːlz ˈɒfn liːdz tuː sɪˈvɪə ˈpʌnɪʃmənt/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Pronounce multi-syllable vocabulary items with correct word stress.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Practise reported speech transformation in spoken form.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Convert this statement into reported speech: 'We must follow the referee's instructions.'
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: The coach explained that we had to follow the referee's instructions.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ðə kəʊtʃ ɪkˈspleɪnd ðæt wiː hæd tuː ˈfɒləʊ ðə ˈrefəriz ɪnˈstrʌkʃnz/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Shift present tense modals to past equivalents when reporting speech.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Demonstrate correct syllable stress on academic and legal vocabulary.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Read aloud: Discipline and regulations are essential for preventing illegal actions.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Discipline and regulations are essential for preventing illegal actions.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ˈdɪsəplɪn ænd ˌreɡjuˈleɪʃnz ɑː ɪˈsenʃl fɔː prɪˈventɪŋ ɪˈliːɡl ˈækʃnz/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Place strong primary stress on the correct syllables for words like dis-ci-pline and reg-u-la-tions.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Demonstrate rising intonation for questions and falling intonation for statements.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Say this question with a rising tone, then answer with a falling tone: Are we allowed to play? No, we aren't.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Are we allowed to play? No, we aren't allowed to play today.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ɑː wiː əˈlaʊd tuː pleɪ? nəʊ, wiː ɑːnt əˈlaʊd tuː pleɪ təˈdeɪ/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use a rising pitch at the end of yes/no questions and a falling pitch at the end of definitive answers.
